$comment: The model lineup for every stage of the loop. `ralph/models.ts` resolves it;
`ralph/README.md` documents it. Change a model HERE, not in a script.
A block is a COMPLETE lineup: naming a loop means spelling out all five
stages, so a block can be read on its own without diffing it against
`default`. `default` is what a loop without its own block runs.
Loop blocks nest under their PROJECT id, because loop names repeat across
projects: { "loggd": { "ralph": {…}, "default": {…} } }. A loop resolves
<project>.<loop>, then <project>.@<role>, then <project>.default, then the
top-level `default`. The project id is RALPH_PROJECT_ID (ralph.sh exports
it), else the directory of the repo's main checkout. A bare loop block at
the top level is refused.
A @<role> key is the project's default lineup for every loop in that role,
so a second triager needs no block of its own. It is complete over THAT
role's stages (`ralph/roles.ts`) and is refused for naming any other: a
triager names orchestrator, mapper and review.spec, and never an executor.
The `default` blocks name all five, because every role falls back to them.
`review.correctness` is the third review axis, a bug hunt over the diff. A
block may leave it out and then runs claude-opus-5-5 at high, so lineups
written before it existed still resolve; every checked-in block names it.
A clerk resolves `orchestrator` and `code-context` (ralph#499): the model its
code-context iterations read the application code with, `claude` only, and
the one stage a block may leave out — it then runs claude-opus-5-5 at high.
Name it in a project's `@clerk` block; every other block refuses it.
Every stage names a RUNNER as well as a model, because a model is only
reachable through a harness that can host it:
orchestrator      claude | codex         owns the iteration
executor          opencode | claude | codex  delegate.sh starts the process
mapper, review.*  claude | opencode | codex
The executor on the `claude` runner is a `claude -p` process under the rails
in `ralph/claude-executor-settings.json`, and takes a FULL model id (never
one of the four aliases) so the usage ledger can attribute what it spent.
On the `claude` runner those last three are named subagents ralph.sh defines
per run (ralph-mapper, ralph-review-standards, ralph-review-spec,
ralph-review-correctness), and take an
alias — opus, sonnet, haiku, fable — or a full claude-… id, plus an optional
`effort`. On any other runner they are a process `ralph/inspect.sh` starts,
and take that harness's own model ids: provider/model for opencode, a bare
id for codex.
A read-only stage on a NON-claude runner may also name `fallback` as an
ordered array of model ids. provider/model ids run through OpenCode, bare
ids through Codex, and opus/sonnet/haiku/fable as an ad-hoc Agent call.
The next route is tried when inspect.sh exits 2 (unavailable) or 4 (failed).
A legacy scalar alias still loads; new edits write the array form. With no
field the chain defaults to ["opus"]. A claude primary takes no fallback
because that stage already runs in-session.
The orchestrator runs on Claude Code or Codex. The rendered prompt routes
Claude inspection stages through external processes when hosted by Codex,
and each runner reports the same supervisor control sigils.
The environment still wins for a one-off: RALPH_MODEL_<STAGE> and
RALPH_RUNNER_<STAGE> for every stage, plus RALPH_MODEL_<STAGE>_EFFORT.
Moving a stage to another harness usually means setting both.
`effort` controls the Claude orchestrator's effort, a named Claude stage
agent's effort, or any Codex stage's reasoning. opencode takes none, and
neither does an executor on `claude` (delegate.sh hands it no effort).
Token accounting accepts every model id. Context occupancy is available
when `ralph/usage.py` knows the model's context window.
$comment_loops: Each named loop in the roster gets a block of its own so it never falls to
`default` unannounced — that is the rule. WHICH model sits in each seat is
not: these blocks are the bench, and moving a stage onto another model or
another runner for a day's comparison is the point of the file. The tests
pin the rule, not the picks, so an experiment costs one edit here and no
test edit.
A `@<role>` default satisfies that rule for every loop in its role: the
stages resolve with source `role`, so nothing falls to `default` unheard,
and a roster the file cannot read — another project's — needs no block per
name. A loop that wants its own lineup still overrides the role block
wholly, exactly as it overrides `default`.
What a comparison needs to stay readable: move one variable at a time and
hold the rest equal across the loops being compared, or a cheaper day says
the lineup is cheaper and never which part of it did the work. The
orchestrator is the usual variable, since it is the stage with an effort
flag and the one that decides the shape of an iteration; the review axes
are the usual thing to hold expensive, because the pre-PR review is often
the only review a change gets, and a reviewer at the executor’s own tier
shares its blind spots.
Anthropic models run through `claude`, OpenCode Go models through
`opencode`; the resolver refuses the crossed pair, so that one is not a
judgement call.
